case.label: D
case.text: A database with small random I/O is the textbook case for Provisioned IOPS SSD, so a candidate could say io2 Block Express is the safe fit. It fails only on cost: 10,000 IOPS is inside what gp3 can provision, and the stem gives no latency or durability constraint that io2 would be needed for. The phrases 'only as far as the workload needs them' (A) and 'kept at that level all day' (D) are mild cost cues, but the IOPS figure decides the answer.

case.label: A
case.text: A daily snapshot copied to a second Region also lets the company rebuild the database after an AZ failure, and it covers more failures than the same-Region snapshot. It meets the stated RPO and RTO. It loses only on cost (second copy plus cross-Region transfer), and the stem asks for MOST cost-effective, so the cost word decides. The snapshot of D is already stored regionally, so it survives the loss of one AZ.

case.label: D
case.text: A gp3 volume gives low latency and survives a stop, so a candidate could call it the standard answer. It loses because the data is scratch that can be re-created, the stem asks for the lowest latency possible, and instance store comes with the instance at no separate storage charge. The cues 'temporary scratch data' and 're-create from S3' point strongly at instance store.

case.label: B
case.text: A candidate who remembers 'EBS persists' could pick B and make no change. It is wrong because the stem states that the root volume disappears under the default settings, and B uses an absolute ('whatever the settings are'). No second option is defensible.

case.label: D
case.text: The Snapshots Archive tier is cheaper per GB and suggests cost savings, but the company only needs the last 7 days, archived snapshots must be restored first and have a minimum period, and nothing says old restore points are worth keeping. Deleting the old snapshots costs less. C and A state wrong dependencies, which also reads as cueing: wrong options carry explicit false claims.

case.label: A
case.text: Restoring a snapshot into a smaller volume looks like the cleanest path, and a candidate who does not know the rule could pick it. It is not possible: a volume made from a snapshot cannot be smaller than the snapshot. This depends on that one rule, which the stem does not state. D also works but costs more than C, so C is unique.

case.label: C
case.text: Multi-Attach on io2 looks like shared block storage for many instances. It fails because the volume is bound to one AZ and the group spans several AZs, and the stem says the solution must survive the loss of one AZ. The phrase 'standard file operations' also cues a file system.

case.label: B
case.text: Pre-reading every block with dd (initialization) is a documented way to remove the first-use penalty, so a candidate could defend B. It adds a script, runs evenings, and the volumes must be created ahead, which means more operational overhead than turning on fast snapshot restore. D does not remove the penalty for snapshot-restored volumes.

case.label: A
case.text: A cron job with the AWS CLI also takes and prunes snapshots and could be paired with E to meet both requirements. It loses on the stem's LEAST operational overhead criterion: per-instance scripts versus a managed Data Lifecycle Manager policy. C and D rest on durability claims that do not replace backups.

case.label: A
case.text: A RAID 1 mirror of two io2 Block Express volumes adds redundancy for a mission-critical database. The stem asks for the highest durability EBS offers, which one io2 Block Express volume already has, and for the MOST cost-effective option, so the second volume is extra cost. The phrase 'mission-critical' might push some candidates to A, but no availability or mirroring requirement is stated.

answers.flag: B leaves the shared copies owned by the production account and encrypted under a production-account key, so a candidate could argue the isolation goal is not fully met, and only C (which copies into a key owned by the backup account) fits that goal, yet C cannot work because snapshots under the AWS managed key cannot be shared.

case.label: C
case.text: Letting the backup account copy the snapshots under its own key gives the strongest isolation, because the copies would then be owned by the backup account and not depend on any production key. C is infeasible as written, because snapshots encrypted with the AWS managed key cannot be shared. B is the best available, but the stem's goal ('a compromise of the production account does not reach the copies') is not fully met by sharing alone, since the production account still owns the snapshots and the key.

case.label: B
case.text: Restoring a snapshot to a larger volume also grows storage and is a familiar approach. It needs a switch of the application to the new volume, which means downtime, and the stem says the application cannot be stopped. Elastic Volumes with a file system extension is the only listed way that avoids downtime.

answers.flag: The stem calls the application 'clustered', so a candidate could argue the application already coordinates its own writes and that C (or A alone) is enough, instead of adding a clustered file system as in E.

case.label: C
case.text: Multi-Attach does not coordinate writes between instances, and if the clustered application is already cluster-aware, it can manage block-level write ordering itself, so A plus custom coordination in C could satisfy the stem. It loses on the 'LEAST operational overhead' phrase, since new code costs more than a ready clustered file system, but the stem does not say the application is not cluster-aware.

case.label: D
case.text: Adding a third volume in RAID 0 sums IOPS and is a well-known approach to scale performance. It fails here because the bottleneck is the instance's EBS limit, which stays the same no matter how many volumes are attached. A fails for the same reason. The stem states the limit directly, so the answer is not hidden.

answers.flag: The stem gives no throughput target, so a candidate could defend gp3 (C): a 2 TiB st1 volume has a modest baseline, and repeated scans many times a day could use up its burst balance, while gp3 can provision throughput.

case.label: C
case.text: A gp3 volume has a baseline throughput that does not depend on burst credits, and throughput can be raised. With 'many times a day' scans on a 2 TiB volume, the st1 burst bucket may not refill and a candidate could argue gp3 meets 'finish quickly' more reliably. St1 is the cheaper type for large sequential reads, which the cues 'large files' and 'sequentially' point to, but the stem has no MiB/s figure to prove it.

case.label: B
case.text: Growing the gp2 volume until its baseline reaches 8,000 IOPS works technically, without a type change. It requires a much larger volume, and the stem says the data stays near 100 GiB, so paying for the extra size costs more than provisioning IOPS on gp3.

case.label: C
case.text: EFS keeps files across stop and start and needs no volume per instance, so a candidate could choose it. It has higher latency and a higher price per GB than gp3, and the stem asks for fast small random I/O and the MOST cost-effective option, so gp3 fits better. B fails because instance store data is lost when the instance stops.

case.label: B
case.text: Governance mode also locks the snapshot for a year and is easier to manage. Users with the right permission can remove a governance lock, and the stem says several administrators have full EC2 access, so only compliance mode gives immutability. The cue 'full access' decides the answer.

case.label: C
case.text: A scheduled Lambda function that replaces unencrypted volumes could be built to enforce the policy for new volumes and covers the existing one too. It is a detective control that runs hourly, leaves a window of unencrypted volumes, and adds code to maintain, so it loses to encryption by default on the LEAST overhead criterion. B and E rest on false claims that an existing volume can be encrypted in place or by the account setting.

case.label: B
case.text: Customer managed keys per Region plus encryption by default also meet the requirement and give more control. They add key creation and management per Region, and the stem does not ask for control over the key, so the option with the AWS managed key has less overhead. A is wrong because the setting is per Region.

case.label: B
case.text: Archive stores a full copy of a snapshot, while standard-tier snapshots are incremental, so if the volume changes little between months the standard tier could cost less. The stem does not give the change rate. A careful reader could use that gap for B, but B is also the unchanged situation the stem wants to improve, and the cues 'infrequently accessed', 'long-term' and 'up to three days acceptable' point to the archive tier.

case.label: A
case.text: A warm standby instance in the second Region would shorten recovery, and a candidate focused on resilience could prefer it. The stem accepts several hours of recovery time and asks for MOST cost-effective, so the cold restore from the copied snapshot in B is enough, and A pays for an idle instance.
